source.title: ATLAS: Adaptive Transfer Scaling Laws for Multilingual Pretraining, Finetuning, and Decoding the Curse of Multilinguality
source.authors: Shayne Longpre; Sneha Kudugunta; Niklas Muennighoff; I-Hung Hsu; Isaac Caswell; Alex Pentland; Sercan Ö. Arik; Chen-Yu Lee; Sayna Ebrahimi

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present. Some tables and figures are flattened in the text extraction, but the relevant reported results are also described in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The study runs multilingual pretraining and fine-tuning scaling experiments and evaluates fitted loss laws, including held-out generalization. It is a conceptual test of scaling-law claims in multilingual settings, rather than a direct reproduction of the original English studies.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the reported fitted pretraining loss laws, held-out scaling-law generalization, optimal scaling trajectories, and the reported fine-tuning comparison. The paper also reports language-transfer scores and capacity effects; those results are not separately rowed unless they directly measure one of the listed claim versions. Related-work results cited from other papers are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study tests held-out language-model loss scaling in multilingual and data-repetition settings, using its own training runs and comparisons of fitted laws. It directly bears on V1, the tested extrapolation component of V2, repeated-data scaling in V5, and setup dependence in V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially correct. The authors conclude that ATLAS improves multilingual loss prediction, multilingual training carries a compute-efficiency tax, increased model capacity mitigates the language-coverage penalty, and scratch-versus-continued-pretraining efficiency depends on budget and language. Its advantage is not uniform across every monolingual evaluation axis. The language-expansion allocations are derived from a fitted law, and the crossover heuristic depends on checkpoint mixture and training duration.
record.recipe_differences: This is a multilingual extension using 774 experiments, multilingual mixtures, data-repetition-aware fitting, and cross-lingual transfer terms; it is not a reproduction of the original English scaling-law experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Fitted coefficients and frontier position vary by language, vocabulary (monolingual or multilingual), training mixture (monolingual or Unimax), and data repetition. The authors also report dependence on which data-source terms are included in the multilingual law.

fits_no_version.finding: Scratch pretraining overtakes continued pretraining from a multilingual checkpoint after 144B–283B additional tokens for the displayed 2B models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The preferred scratch-versus-warm-start training strategy depends on language, adaptation budget and checkpoint history.

fits_no_version.finding: The fitted language-coverage law yields parameter, token and compute multipliers for preserving loss when adding languages.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Starting from the assumed compute-optimal baseline, expanding coverage by r requires the study's derived iso-loss compute multiplier r^0.970.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 1 compares the position and shape of optimal parameter/data trajectories across languages and training regimes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Vocabulary, multilingual training and repetition change the allocation trajectory required to reach a given loss.

record.problems: The study reports fit metrics and selected held-out results, but does not provide uncertainty estimates for the scaling-law coefficients in the reported text. Some reported plots are difficult to inspect from the flattened extraction. The authors note that pretraining-versus-finetuning crossover points depend on the multilingual checkpoint's mixture and training duration.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-version results were intentionally omitted. Language-pair transfer matrices and most capacity-curve details were not rowed because they do not measure a listed version's stated outcome; the relevant language-expansion iso-loss findings are summarized in R30–R31.

untested.parts: The tabled formulas alone do not independently establish non-bottleneck scaling over several orders of magnitude separately for parameters, tokens and compute.
Prediction of runs orders of magnitude larger than all runs used for fitting. Holding out 8B while retaining other multi-billion-parameter sizes does not establish that scale separation.
An empirical test that loss-minimising parameter and token counts each follow stable powers of a fixed compute budget, including the Kaplan-versus-Hoffmann allocation comparison.
Controlled architecture-shape changes at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities and a power-law loss-form test for fine-tuning or transfer. The scratch-versus-continued-pretraining crossover is a different outcome.
Downstream task performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
Controlled changes to parameter-count conventions, training schedules and optimizers, and a direct explanation of disagreement between the original published allocation laws.

missing.what: Separate multilingual largest-model results: CSL R2(N)=-0.99, MSL=-0.65 and target-data-only ATLAS=-0.75. These explicit extrapolation failures are not captured by the mixture-only comparator rows.

Separate held-out token and compute results for monolingual laws: CSL R2(D)=0.94 and R2(C)=0.90; DCSL 0.93 and 0.88; ATLAS 0.91 and 0.88. ATLAS's advantage is specific to held-out model size in this setting.

Separate multilingual data-term ablation rows: adding Dother changes R2(N) from -0.75 to 0.89, R2(D) from 0.80 to 0.97 and R2(C) from 0.72 to 0.97; adding explicit transfer languages changes R2(M) from 0.66 to 0.82.

record.verdict_notes: Use the supplied text only. Table 1 and prose disagree on CSL/MSL mixture scores: 0.61/0.70 versus 0.64/0.69. Section 6 and Figure 7 also contain inconsistent crossover-fit coefficients, exponents and a log(C) expression; they do not establish a power-law loss form for fine-tuning. The main text says the base checkpoint used 1B tokens, whereas B.4 and B.5 specify 1T. No V3 or V5 verdict should be based merely on a missing exponent or an untested modality.

versions.untested_parts: The paper tests multilingual and monolingual text loss across its stated language, model-size, token, vocabulary, and training-mixture settings; it does not establish the law for all language models or all possible settings.
Generalization is evaluated on held-out model sizes, token ranges, compute runs, and language mixtures in this study's experimental ranges; no extrapolation beyond those tests is established.

The paper reports optimal scaling trajectories across language and training regimes, but does not give a general fixed-compute parameter/token allocation law directly comparable to the Kaplan-versus-Hoffmann comparison. Its explicit compute-optimal derivation concerns adding languages while preserving loss.
No controlled sweep of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study is limited to text multilingual pretraining and monolingual continued pretraining from multilingual checkpoints; it does not test image, video, or other modalities.
No downstream task performance scaling is reported.

The study tests differences by language, vocabulary/training regime, data repetition, and fitted law. It does not systematically vary all fitting choices named in the version, such as alternative parameter-count conventions.

rows.subject: Monolingual model scaling-law fits across six languages
rows.operation_detail: Compare fitted monolingual loss curves across English, French, Russian, Chinese, Hindi, and Swahili
rows.measure: Similarity of optimal scaling-curve exponents and returns
rows.value: The curves are described as nearly parallel, with similar exponents and comparable returns to additional data and parameters.
rows.note: Reported as an across-language qualitative comparison.
rows.check: This records qualitative consistency across languages, rather than evidence of fit dependence. Do not interpret nearly parallel as identical exponents: Table C.1 reports monolingual exponents from 0.26 to 0.64.

source_check.locator_found: Figure 1 and Section 3, paragraph comparing monolingual scaling trajectories.

rows.subject: Hindi and Swahili monolingual scaling curves
rows.operation_detail: Observe loss curves as training tokens increase into repeated-data regimes
rows.measure: Shape of right tail of loss curves
rows.value: The curves bend upward at the right tail, described as consistent with diminishing returns from severe data repetition after many epochs.
rows.note: The reported behavior qualifies a single power law when training enters severe repetition.
rows.check: Figure 1 plots optimal model-size/data trajectories, not loss curves. Its upward bend indicates diminishing returns to repeated tokens, not an observed increase in loss. Severe repetition tests V5; it does not violate V1's non-bottleneck condition. The departure is observed evidence for V7.

rows.subject: Monolingual and multilingual training scaling frontiers
rows.operation_detail: Compare optimal loss frontiers under changes to vocabulary and training mixture

conditions.value: monolingual vocabulary/monolingual data; multilingual vocabulary/monolingual data; multilingual vocabulary/Unimax data

rows.measure: Relative compute efficiency and frontier position
rows.value: Both multilingual vocabulary and Unimax training shift the frontier upward; the compute-efficiency tax is most pronounced for English.
rows.note: The multilingual regimes retain scaling trajectories but have a loss/efficiency penalty relative to the stated baseline.
rows.check: The compute-efficiency tax is a setup-dependent frontier shift, not incomplete power-law behavior. Figure 1 shows model-size/data allocation trajectories rather than a direct loss-versus-compute frontier.

rows.subject: ATLAS (Dt + Dother + Kt Di), multilingual fits in this study
rows.operation_detail: Fit ATLAS with target-language, other-language, and transfer-language data terms; evaluate held-out dimensions

conditions.value: model size, token range, compute, and language mixtures

rows.baseline: Existing compared laws; exact values are not stated for every dimension in the prose
rows.value: The text reports that ATLAS frequently achieves > 0.9 fit and outperforms the other laws across all held-out dimensions; R2(M) = 0.82.
rows.note: The text explicitly attributes reliable out-of-sample multilingual generalization to ATLAS and says the transfer-language term is needed to exceed MSL on mixture generalization.
rows.check: Split the combined measures: full multilingual ATLAS has R2(N)=0.89, R2(D)=0.96, R2(C)=0.98 and R2(M)=0.82 in Table 1. Only N, D and C test scale extrapolation; M tests mixture generalization. Orders-of-magnitude extrapolation is not established.

source_check.correct: Table 1 states all comparator values. In axis order R²(N), R²(D), R²(C), R²(M): CSL=(-0.99,0.72,0.66,0.61); MSL=(-0.65,0.73,0.67,0.70); target-data-only ATLAS=(-0.75,0.80,0.72,0.64); ATLAS with target and other-language terms=(0.89,0.97,0.97,0.66). Full ATLAS=(0.89,0.96,0.98,0.82).

rows.subject: Optimal scaling trajectories across language regimes
rows.operation_detail: Compare optimal parameter/data scaling trajectories across languages and training regimes

conditions.value: English, French, Russian, Chinese, Hindi, and Swahili
monolingual vocabulary/monolingual training; multilingual vocabulary/monolingual training; multilingual vocabulary/Unimax training

rows.value: The paper describes per-language optimal trajectories as similar; multilingual vocabulary and Unimax training shift the frontier upward.
rows.note: The text describes trajectory similarity, but does not state a general fixed-compute allocation exponent in the figure caption.
rows.check: Similarity and displacement of fitted optimal trajectories do not measure whether optimal N and D each grow as stable powers of compute. The absence of reported allocation exponents is untested scope, not a V3 limitation result. The setup shifts duplicate R21.

rows.subject: Monolingual scratch-pretraining versus Unimax-checkpoint continued-pretraining curves
rows.size_stated: 2B-parameter models in Figure 6; experiments also span multiple model scales
rows.stage_stated: pretraining and continued pretraining (called finetuning in the paper)
rows.operation_detail: Compare interpolated target-language loss curves for scratch pretraining and continued pretraining from a multilingual checkpoint

conditions.value: eight languages, including English, Japanese, Portuguese, German, Russian, Vietnamese, Spanish, and Chinese

rows.measure: Training-token crossover at which scratch pretraining has lower loss
rows.value: Scratch pretraining surpasses the warm-started model after 144B–283B tokens, depending on language; finetuning is usually more efficient below 144B tokens and scratch pretraining at budgets of ≥ 283B tokens.
rows.note: This compares text continued-pretraining and scratch-pretraining loss curves, but does not establish that the same power-law form holds in every fine-tuning or transfer setting.
rows.check: The crossover values are supported for the displayed 2B models, but comparing scratch and continued-pretraining loss does not test a power-law loss form in continued pretraining. Do not label V5 from this comparison.

rows.subject: Multilingual capacity scaling-law fit across languages
rows.operation_detail: Fit language loss as a function of model size, target-language tokens, and number of languages

conditions.value: eight individual languages and combined language data

rows.value: For the fit on all language data, ϕ = 0.11 and ψ = −0.04; the selected form achieved robust R2 ≥ 0.87.
rows.note: Related multilingual-capacity result; it is not the fixed-language-count compute-optimal parameter/token allocation in V3.
rows.check: This is a held-out pretraining-loss law with power-law N and D terms conditional on language count, so it bears on V1. The reported pooled fit is R2≥0.87; individual-language fits are reported above 0.8. The coverage exponents alone do not test V3.

source_check.locator_found: Section 5, multilingual capacity law and pooled coefficients; Subsection B.7.1, Equation 7.

rows.subject: Multilingual capacity iso-loss allocation
rows.operation_detail: Derive how parameter count, tokens, and compute should change to add languages while preserving per-language loss
rows.measure: Iso-loss multipliers for parameters, total tokens, and compute
rows.baseline: Original coverage K and its loss
rows.value: For 4·K languages, total tokens increase by 2.74 and model size by 1.4; computed compute-budget scaling is C·r^0.970.
rows.note: This is an allocation result for changing language coverage at constant loss, not the fixed-coverage compute-optimal split specified in V3.
rows.check: The numerical multipliers match the reported derivation. They concern increasing language coverage at constant loss, not fixed-coverage allocation as compute increases in V3. They are derived predictions, not independent experimental validation; the appendix's final optimum assumes a compute-optimal baseline.
